seo.title: Karmic tail 3 16 22 compatibility: The Empress, The Tower, The Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 16 22 compatibility: why it forms only when both partners have the tail 15-8-11, and what such a couple can never gamble away.

title: Karmic tail 3-16-22 in compatibility: what a couple cannot gamble away
short: The couple's karmic tail 3-16-22 looks like a verdict: The Empress builds a house, The Tower knocks it down, The Fool walks off with nothing. In compatibility these three cards tell a different story: how a couple stripped of everything external recognise each other by what cannot be taken.

sections.h2: A tale told to someone who has lost everything
paragraphs: In the third book of the Mahabharata, King Yudhishthira sits in the forest dressed in deerskins. He has lost his wealth and his kingdom at dice, his wife has been dragged before the assembly in disgrace, and long years of exile lie ahead. He puts to the sage Brihadashva the question anyone asks when their house has fallen: "Is there a king on this earth who is more unfortunate than myself?"

The sage answers with a story. There was a king called Nala — handsome, a master of horses, truthful and generous. There was a princess called Damayanti, more beautiful than any god or mortal had seen. They fell in love without meeting, through what others told them, and golden messenger birds brought them together. She chose him over the gods; for twelve years they lived happily and had a son and a daughter. Then Nala lost everything to his brother at dice, down to his last garment, went into the forest with his wife, left her asleep, was turned into an ugly man by a serpent, served as a stableman to a foreign king — and in the fourth year his wife recognised him by the taste of the food he had cooked.

In India this is one of the best-loved tales. In Europe generations began learning Sanskrit with it: Franz Bopp published "Nala" with a Latin translation in 1819, and textbooks placed it first. In Russian the tale was retold by Vasily Zhukovsky in 1844, from Friedrich Rückert's German version, and in 1904 the Bolshoi Theatre staged Anton Arensky's opera "Nal and Damayanti" to a libretto by Modest Tchaikovsky.

For the tail 3-16-22 something else matters more. The tale's three acts run exactly in the order of the three cards: the choice and the flourishing kingdom — The Empress; the game of dice — The Tower; the forest, nakedness and the road — The Fool. And it is told not as a prophecy but as a remedy, to a man for whom everything has already happened.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Empress who chose a mortal
paragraphs: A svayamvara is a ceremony at which the bride herself chooses a husband from the assembled suitors. Kings came to Damayanti's svayamvara, and so did four gods. The gods wanted her for themselves, and when they learned that she loved Nala, they took on his form. Damayanti entered the hall and saw "five persons all alike in appearance".

The marks of the gods that her elders had told her about showed on none of them. So she prayed: "For the sake of truth, O, let the gods reveal him to me." The gods assumed their own attributes. They do not sweat, they do not blink, their garlands do not fade, no dust settles on them, and they stand without touching the ground. Ganguli's translation puts it this way: she beheld "the celestials unmoistened with perspiration, with winkless eyes, and unfading garlands, unstained with dust, and staying without touching the ground", while Nala "stood revealed to his shadow, his fading garlands, himself stained with dust and sweat, resting on the ground with winking eyes". She chose the one with a shadow, sweat and a wilting garland. Nala answered with a vow: "Since thou, O blessed one, hast chosen a mortal in the presence of the celestials, know me for a husband even obedient to thy command."

That choice contains the whole Empress at the entry to the couple's tail. What these two want together is not an ideal but a living, earthly life where everything grows and everything wilts: a home that smells of cooking, a garden that needs watering, children, guests, a shared venture. The couple fill their life remarkably fast. Within six months a rented flat becomes a home, plants climb up the windowsills, people gather at weekends, and both enjoy having plenty around them.

For Lisovskaya, the entry point of the couple's tail stands for shared wishes, agreements and a "common language". In the reading on the site the same 3 also stands at the end of the line "Relationship and common language": this couple's language is the language of home. They easily agree on a renovation, a trip or a celebration, and find it hard to talk about the possibility of losing the home.

The wish is strong because it is doubled. Each partner brings The Devil — 15 — into the couple, the card of a strong personal "I want", of attachment and passion. Two fifteens make thirty, and thirty folds into three: two wishes to possess add up to a wish to grow. But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that such a wish can turn into resistance. The Empress in the minus is a home to be preserved at any cost, money that comes in "feast or famine", a jealous count of which of the two has grown and which has fallen behind.

At the wedding of Nala and Damayanti the gods gave gifts, and they are worth remembering: they will be needed at the end. Fire comes whenever Nala wishes, water wherever he desires, his garlands keep their celestial fragrance, and his food gains a subtle taste. The kings rode away and Nala took his wife home. Zhukovsky describes their happiness like this: he lived "drop by drop drinking life from a single cup together with her" (our translation).

sections.h2: Middle of the task: The Tower that waited twelve years
paragraphs: One more suitor arrived late for the svayamvara: Kali, the spirit of strife and of the losing throw at dice. Learning that Damayanti had chosen a mortal in the presence of the gods, he swore revenge and settled in Nala's kingdom. He waited for a crack to open in the righteous king, "always watching for a hole". In the Mahabharata he had to wait twelve years (in Zhukovsky, six). One day Nala said his evening prayers "without having previously washed his feet", and Kali entered him through that tiny lapse.

From here on it is The Tower card at work. Nala's brother Pushkara challenged him to play, and Nala could not refuse for long: "Thus challenged in the presence of Damayanti, the lofty-minded king could not long decline it." He lost gold, chariots and robes, and the more he lost, the hotter he burned. The citizens came to the gate, Damayanti passed on their pleas, and he did not say a word. The people went home saying, "He liveth not." The game went on for many months.

Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe" and reads it as "the ruin of the House of Life, when evil has prevailed therein". In Wen the key word is suddenness: "What seemed stable and solid to the Seeker is not so; it is in fact destructible." But the tale holds a detail that changes everything. When the sage first describes Nala, among his virtues — truthful, a master of horses, commander of a mighty army — stands one more: "fond of dice". The crack was in the very first line, among the virtues. The catastrophe looks unforeseen only to those who skipped the first line.

In a couple's life the Tower in the middle rarely looks like a bolt from the blue. More often one of the two disappears headlong into something — work, a project, a principle, a grievance, a game of any kind — while the other knocks at a closed door and hears no answer. The house falls not in a day but over "many months", and the whole time both hope the next throw will put things right. Among The Tower's tasks Lisovskaya gives an exact description of this picture: in bad times the partners look in different directions. There is another one too: the collapse of an imagined image of the partner. Nala, whom Damayanti chose because he stood on the ground, suddenly turns out to be possessed, deaf and a stranger.

Why The Tower stands in the middle of the tail can be seen from the numbers. Each partner brings Justice — 8 — into the couple: their own scales and their own sense of what is right. Eight plus eight is sixteen: two versions of "this is the right way" meet in one house. Nala does not sit down to play out of greed: the challenge was thrown in front of his wife, and a king's honour forbids refusing. In a couple this looks familiar: each acts by their own code of honour, and at some point the two codes strike each other like lightning striking the top of a tower.

Inside The Tower the tale also shows the card's plus. Damayanti does not wait for it all to end. She calls the charioteer, puts the children into a chariot drawn by her husband's favourite horses and sends them to her father. Lisovskaya writes of The Tower in a couple: the ability to take serious decisions quickly and calm in unexpected trouble. And one more detail: Damayanti refuses to name a culprit. "I do not think," she says, "that in this the high-souled Naishadha is to blame."

The last throw matters as well. When everything is lost, Pushkara laughingly offers to stake Damayanti. Nala silently takes off his ornaments and leaves the city in a single garment. That is where The Tower stopped: he did not stake a person.

sections.h2: Main task: The Fool whose last garment the birds took
paragraphs: Nala and Damayanti spent three nights outside the city walls: Pushkara proclaimed that anyone who helped them would be put to death. Then they went into the forest and lived on roots. One day the hungry Nala saw some birds with golden plumage and thought they would be his meal and his wealth. He threw his last garment over them, and the birds rose into the sky with it. From above they spoke, in Ganguli's translation:
"O thou of small sense, we are even those dice. We had come hither wishing to take away thy cloth, for it pleased us not that thou shouldst depart even with thy cloth on."

That is how The Fool is born: a naked man at the edge of the forest, called a fool by his own dice — and in Zhukovsky the dice even sing him off with "farewell, reckless one; a happy journey!" (our translation). At the beginning of the tale golden birds brought love: Nala caught one and let it go, and it flew off to tell Damayanti about him. At the end golden birds carried off his last possession: these he tried to hold on to. For Waite The Fool is zero, the card without a number. Nala reached zero literally.

The Fool as the main task is not about irresponsibility as such. It is about what two people do when they have nothing. Wen writes of The Fool as a fork: "One fork will lead to attainment (flying, transcending the cliff) and the other will lead to likely demise (falling off the cliff)." Nala points out the fork at once. He starts explaining the roads to Damayanti: this one leads south, this one to the mountains, and this one to her father's country. She understands before he does where he is heading: why are you showing me the way? And she replies that "in every sorrow there is no physic equal unto the wife". Nala agrees and promises not to part from her.

Next comes the image that makes the whole tale worth reading. The two of them have one cloth between them: Damayanti covers her husband with half of her own garment, and they walk on "both attired in one cloth". This is the couple's Fool in the plus: two people who own nothing but one piece of cloth and each other — and that is enough to keep walking.

And here is The Fool in the minus. At night in an empty shelter Nala cannot sleep and reasons: she will be better off without me, she will go back to her family, and with me only grief awaits her. He finds a blade lying unsheathed near the shelter, cuts their shared cloth in half and leaves. Then he comes back, weeps over her as she sleeps, leaves again. Ganguli's translation compares him to a swing, "dragged away by Kali but drawn back by love"; Zhukovsky has him pulled "now by the mighty foe, now by love" (our translation). In the end he goes.

Here another clue from the numbers shows up. The centre of the matrix in every couple with this tail is 8, Justice, without exception. The atmosphere inside such a couple is a pair of scales: fair, equal, each paying their own way. That is a strength as long as the subject is the budget and the chores. But in the tale the blade appears at the most terrible moment and works like the sword of Justice: the cloth is divided exactly in half so that the two can part. The most dangerous thing this tail knows how to do is to split everything equally and leave "for the other's good". Among The Fool's tasks Lisovskaya names running away from problems and a couple who seem to be together but do everything separately and live like neighbours. Nala decided for both of them what was best for Damayanti and did not ask her.

The separation in the tale is Kali's doing, and there is no need to repeat it. But in the forest each of the two shows a Strength of their own. The personal tails of both partners end with card 11, Strength: the ability to endure, to face the beast and not back away. Eleven twice is twenty-two, The Fool.

Damayanti walks alone through a forest full of tigers. A tiger comes out to meet her and she decides: "Even him will I accost fearlessly" — and asks the king of beasts whether he has seen Nala. Meanwhile Nala hears a voice from a burning forest, "O righteous Nala, come hither", walks into the flames saying "Fear not", and carries out the serpent Karkotaka. The serpent bites him and changes his form. In Zhukovsky the serpent explains: "You are transformed, you have parted with yourself, and from now on, as nobody, you cannot be recognised even by your own wife" (our translation).

Our reading: two Strengths in one couple make not a double wall but a road. When both know how to endure and hold on, there is nothing left to hold — what remains is to walk. Lisovskaya describes The Fool in the plus as a couple where each is self-sufficient, where trust brings a great deal of freedom, and where starting from zero comes easily. The tale shows where this lightness comes from: each of the two learned separately that they would hold out. She learned to search and to act; he learned to serve and to be nobody.

Nala becomes Bahuka (Vahuka in Ganguli's translation): "of unsightly appearance and possessed of short arms", as the text says, a stableman and cook at the court of King Rituparna. That court never had a better stableman. Every evening he recites a verse about the woman who is hungry and worn out somewhere in the forest. When a companion asks whom he is weeping for, Nala tells his own story in the third person: "A certain person devoid of sense had a wife." The Fool calls himself by his own name.

sections.h2: Recognition: what The Tower could not take
paragraphs: Meanwhile Damayanti had returned to her father and sent Brahmins out to every kingdom. At every court they repeated her words: "O beloved gambler, where hast thou gone cutting off half of my garment, and deserting the dear and devoted wife asleep in the forest?" Only one man answered — the short-armed stableman. He spoke up for the runaway: a wife "should not be angry with one that was deprived by birds of his garment while striving to procure sustenance". Only Nala knew about the birds.

To bring him back, Damayanti announced that tomorrow she would choose a husband again. Only someone who drove horses like Nala could arrive within a single day. Bahuka carried King Rituparna to her city, and Damayanti sent her maid to watch what this man did. The maid came back amazed. Low doorways rise up before him by themselves. Empty vessels fill with water as soon as he looks at them. A handful of grass bursts into flame in his hand. He touches fire and is not burnt. Flowers pressed in his palms do not crumple but grow fresher, and in Zhukovsky a withered rose comes back to life in his hand.

This is the answer to the tail's riddle. Zhukovsky names it outright: "these were clear signs of Nala, these were the gifts he had received from the gods on his very wedding day, and she… saw with her heart the longed-for Nala where her eyes still saw Vahuka" (our translation). Damayanti arranged the last test herself: she asked for a piece of meat cooked by Bahuka, tasted it and recognised the flavour. A subtle taste in food was also a wedding gift. In Zhukovsky the serpent had already reminded Nala in the forest of "the elemental gifts received from the gods on your wedding day; they are not lost to you" (our translation).

The dice took the kingdom, the clothes and even his face. They did not take the wedding gifts: what was received at the entry to the tail survived The Tower and became the way to recognise each other at zero. Waite says something strange about Justice, the card at the centre of this couple. He separates the law that deals unto every man according to his works from spiritual justice, which is like the possession of gifts: "we have them or have not". The law of stakes takes away whatever has been staked. A gift is never put on the table.

For the couple 3-16-22 this is the main discovery. Their Empress is not a flat or furniture. It is the ability of the two of them to make life around them alive: to feed, to warm, to fill, to bring the withered back. The Tower can take the walls, the job, the familiar way of life and the familiar image of each other. It does not take the ability to make things grow, and by it the two recognise each other when everything external is already lost.

The tale tells the rest quickly. Damayanti calls the wind, the sun and the moon to witness, and the wind answers from the sky: she is pure. In Ganguli's translation the wind sums it up in words as symmetrical as the scales at the centre: "thou hast obtained Bhima's daughter, and she hath also obtained thee." Nala puts on the garment the serpent gave him and regains his former form. They spend the night telling each other what each of them lived through in the forest. Zhukovsky writes that "the living tale of what they had suffered apart" became shared, and "the sad true stories turned into a merry tale" (our translation). The Fool's main task is solved not by a return to the old palace but by the forest becoming a shared story.

sections.h2: The Chariot missing from the tail
paragraphs: If 3-16-22 were a personal tail, the middle would come out differently: in the personal matrix the middle is the folded sum of the two ends, and 3 + 22 = 25 → 7, The Chariot. In the couple's tail that place belongs to The Tower. The Chariot does appear in the tale after all — but after The Tower, not instead of it.

Nala drives someone else's chariot. The lean horses he picked fall to their knees at the first jolt; he raises them with the reins, and they race so fast the chariot seems to fly. On the way King Rituparna's upper garment blows off and the king asks to turn back. Nala answers: "The sheet is dropped down far away. We have travelled one yojana thence. Therefore, it is incapable of being recovered." The third lost garment in the tale — and this time nobody goes back for it.

Then the king boasts that at a glance he has counted the leaves and fruits on a vibhitaka tree. Nala fells the tree, counts, finds the king right and proposes an exchange: his art of horses for the king's art of dice. At the very moment Nala grasps the secret of the game, Kali leaves him and hides in that same vibhitaka. In Zhukovsky the tree withers on the spot.

The detail is no accident. Vibhitaka nuts were India's ancient dice. The gambler's hymn of the Rigveda (X.34), one of the oldest texts about gambling, opens by praising these nuts, "sprung from tall trees on windy heights", and towards the end passes on the advice of the god Savitr: "Play not with dice, cultivate your corn-land… There are your cattle, there your wife, O gambler" (Griffith's translation, revised after Macdonell). The quarrel between The Empress and The Tower was written down some three thousand years ago: the cornfield against the dice.

Our reading is this: speed, command of direction and the ability to steer come to this couple not before the collapse but after it — and as service, not as ownership. Nala drives a chariot that is not his, and that is exactly how he wins back what is his.

sections.h2: The three cards according to Waite: a cornfield, lightning and the edge of a cliff
paragraphs: The cards in the reading are drawn for the site and have their own pictures. Waite describes his cards in words, and the tale of Nala can be recognised in those descriptions.

Waite writes of his Empress: "A field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water." It is the very cornfield Savitr advises ploughing instead of gambling, and the water that by a god's gift fills Nala's vessels. Above all, for Waite, The Empress is "universal fecundity". The entry to the couple's tail is exactly that: two people enter a shared life through the wish to make it grow.

Waite's Tower is struck by lightning, and of the two falling figures he writes: "The one is the literal word made void and the other its false interpretation." The tale has two such empty words: "a king does not refuse a challenge" and "she will be better off without me". Both sound noble, and both bring the house down.

Waite places his own Fool at the brink of a precipice: "The edge which opens on the depth has no terror." But in his historical survey he also recounts an older design: the Fool does not know he is on the brink of a precipice, "but a dog or other animal—some call it a tiger—is attacking him from behind, and he is hurried to his destruction unawares." The tale has both Fools. Nala, driven by Kali, does not see the edge. Damayanti walks up to the tiger herself and speaks to it without fear.
Now for the numbers — checked by running every date through the site's engine.

The tail 3-16-22 occurs in roughly one couple in 563 (0.178%) and ranks 76th of the 97 couple tails. It forms in one way only: both partners have the same personal tail, 15-8-11 — The Devil, Justice, Strength. A person has that tail roughly once in 24 cases. Couples in which both partners have it produce 3-16-22.
Each point of the couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, folded down to 22. Here all three numbers are doublings:

The example: 14.10.1976 and 14.10.1976, two people born on the same day. Each has the personal tail 15-8-11 and centre 4, The Emperor. In the couple's matrix the tail is 3-16-22, the centre is 8 and the couple's values are 6.

Centre 8, Justice, appears in 100% of such couples, and the reason is in the numbers too. Everyone with the tail 15-8-11 has 4, The Emperor, at the centre of their personal matrix, without exception. Four plus four is eight. Our reading: two people, each used to being master of their own life, create between them an atmosphere of scales — respect, fair division and an endless weighing of who has given how much.

The middle, 16, is itself what makes the tail impossible in a personal matrix. There the middle is calculated from the ends: 3 + 22 → 7. Here it is added up from the partners' middles, 8 + 8. That is why The Chariot, which would be "due" under the personal formula, gives way to The Tower in the couple's tail.

There is also a clue visible right in the couple's reading. The "Compatibility of characters" sphere checks whether one partner's point of wishes sounds in the other's chart. In these couples that point is the same for both: 15, The Devil. So every reading of a couple with the tail 3-16-22 shows a match in wishes: the same "I want" in both. Added together, it produces The Empress at the entry.

And the tale, as if it knew, is built entirely of pairs. Five identical Nalas at the svayamvara. Golden birds at the beginning and at the end. Two children — a son, Indrasena, and a daughter, Indrasenā: one name for two, told apart in Sanskrit by a single long vowel. Two bride's choices — a real one and a pretended one. Two kings who trade their arts: horses for dice. And the formula with which the messenger bird brings the lovers together: "The union of the best with the best is happy."

There are no couple tails made of the same three numbers in another order: 3-16-22 is the only one. The partners' personal tail 15-8-11 is read by its own rules, and its conclusions do not carry over to the couple's tail: the couple has different points and different roles.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a choice made again
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, "what your union exists for". In 93.2% of couples with the tail 3-16-22 this is 6, The Lovers. Waite's divinatory list for this card contains words that read like a summary of the tale: "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome." The old Lovers card, he writes, "is said to have been entitled Simulacrum fidei, the symbol of conjugal faith".

The Lovers is a card of choice, and in the tale the choice is made twice. The first time Damayanti chooses a mortal over the gods. The second time she announces a new svayamvara — not to choose someone else but to call the same man back. When they meet, Nala bitterly asks whether any devoted wife could seek a second husband. She answers with the words of her first choice: "passing over the celestials themselves, I choose thee as my lord." This couple's value is a choice that is not made once and for all but confirmed after every loss.

In 6.8% of couples the values are 15, The Devil — the very card with which both partners' personal tails begin. For these couples the bond itself, passion and attachment, is the highest value. The task is to keep the bond from becoming a chain: in the gambler's hymn the dice "give gifts like boys [do], and then snatch them back from the winner" (Griffith's translation, revised after Macdonell).

sections.h2: How karmic tail 3-16-22 lives in a couple: the circle and the way out
paragraphs: In the minus the circle usually runs like this. First the two build abundance and enjoy it. A small crack remains in the foundation — something "we don't discuss": one partner's passion, the other's code of honour, an old grievance, a habit of escaping into work. One day something big enters through that crack, and one of the two stops hearing. The other knocks, then saves what can be saved. Once the house has fallen, the couple at zero faces The Fool's two temptations: to scatter "so as not to be a burden", or to stay under one roof but live apart, like neighbours.

In the plus the circle looks different. A couple that has already lost everything once without losing each other starts from zero more easily than almost anyone: they know their wealth is not in the walls. Such a pair can turn misfortune into a shared story and later tell it with laughter. They are recognisable by the way life starts growing around them again.
What helps this couple:

ul: name the crack aloud while it is small: whatever has gone unspoken in the house for years is exactly where The Tower will come in;
agree in advance on what is never staked — in an argument, with money, in the heat of a game: each couple has its own list, but a person is never on it;
in trouble, do not decide for the other what would be better for them: Nala left "for her good" and never asked her;
do not split everything in half at a moment of fear: the scales at the centre are good for the budget and the chores, not for running away;
look after the gifts, not just the property: what each can do with their hands and heart outlives any loss;
after a hard period, tell each other your "forest" — what each of you went through alone — so that it becomes a shared story rather than a secret.

paragraphs: If the "game" in a couple is a real addiction, debt or a threat to safety, it is no longer a question of cards: specialist help is needed, and in danger, the emergency services.

intro: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** The couple's shared wish is a life that grows: a home, plenty, beauty, children or a joint venture. The couple enters the task through this wish, and the same wish later resists change.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The road from the wish to the task runs through the collapse of whatever rested on habit and on an imagined picture. More often it is not a blow from outside but a crack nobody noticed for years.

**Main task — 22, The Fool.** To learn freedom and trust without a safety net: to start from zero together, not to run from each other, and not to split everything in half when things get frightening.

This tail holds a riddle that others do not. It is formed only by two people with the same personal tail, 15-8-11, so every card of the couple turns out to be one person's card doubled. And its plot is told best of all in an ancient Indian tale about King Nala and Princess Damayanti.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 3-16-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail: the entry to the task is The Empress (the shared wish to grow a home and a life), the middle is The Tower (the collapse of what rested on habit and image), and the main task is The Fool (freedom and trust without a safety net, the ability to start from zero together and not run from each other).

faq.q: Does The Tower in the middle of the couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events. The Tower in the middle describes what the couple goes through on the way to its task: a review of what was built on habit. How and when this is lived through, and whether it is turbulent at all, the cards do not say.

faq.q: Why does this tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the folded sum of the ends: 3 + 22 → 7. Here the middle is 16, added up from the two partners' middles (8 + 8), so the order 3-16-22 is possible only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: If both partners have the tail 15-8-11, does the couple have the same tasks?
faq.a: No. The personal tail 15-8-11 is read by the rules of the personal matrix, and the couple's tail by its own. The match between the personal tails only explains where the couple's numbers come from: each of its cards is one partner's card doubled.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The numbers 3, 16 and 22 form only one order in a couple: 3-16-22. No other arrangement of these numbers exists among couple tails.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail calculated?
faq.a: Calculate both partners' personal matrices and add up the matching points of the tail, folding any sum above 22 by adding its digits. For example, two people born on 14.10.1976 have personal tails 15-8-11, which give the couple's tail 3-16-22. The compatibility calculator does it more conveniently.

report: A wife recognised her husband by the taste of the meat he had cooked. His face was a stranger's, his name was a stranger's, he worked as a stableman for a foreign king, yet his gift was the same. The scene comes from the tale of Nala and Damayanti in the Mahabharata, and it holds the answer to the couple's tail 3-16-22. The tale's three acts run exactly in the order of the three cards: the flourishing kingdom — The Empress; the game of dice — The Tower; the forest and nakedness — The Fool.

At the ceremony where the bride chooses her own husband, four gods came to Damayanti, and all of them took on Nala's form. She saw "five persons all alike in appearance", prayed, and when the gods assumed their own attributes, she told the real one apart by earthly marks. The gods do not sweat, their garlands do not fade, they stand without touching the ground. Nala, in Ganguli's translation, "stood revealed to his shadow, his fading garlands, himself stained with dust and sweat, resting on the ground".

That choice holds the whole Empress at the entry to the task. What a couple with this tail wants together is not an ideal but a living, earthly life where everything grows and everything wilts: a home that smells of cooking, guests, children, a shared venture. Such a pair fill their life remarkably fast. Their common language is the language of home: a renovation or a celebration is easy to agree on, the possibility of losing the home is hard to talk about. The wish is doubled: each partner brings a strong personal "I want", The Devil, into the couple, and together they add up to a wish to make things grow. But the same wish later resists change.
At the wedding the gods gave Nala gifts: fire comes at his will, water wherever he desires, and his food gains a subtle taste. These gifts will be needed later.

report.h3: A crack awaited for twelve years

report: Kali, the spirit of strife and of the losing throw, arrived late for the bride's choice and swore revenge. For twelve years he waited for a crack to open in the righteous king, and he entered Nala through a single lapse. Nala's brother challenged him to play, and months later the kingdom was lost. The citizens stood at the gate, his wife passed on their pleas, the king did not answer.

Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". Yet in the very first description of Nala, among his virtues, stand the words "fond of dice". **The crack was in the first line.** In a couple's life the Tower in the middle rarely looks like a bolt from the blue. More often one partner disappears headlong into work, a principle, a grievance or a game of any kind, while the other knocks at a closed door. Each brings their own scales into the couple — two Justices — and The Tower rises where two versions of "this is the right way" strike each other: Nala sits down to play because a king's honour forbids refusing a challenge.

Inside The Tower the tale also shows its plus. Damayanti sends the children to her father while her husband is still playing, and refuses to name a culprit. And when the brother offers to stake her herself, Nala silently leaves the city in a single garment. **He did not stake a person.**

report.h3: Dice that wish a happy journey

report: In the forest the hungry Nala throws his last garment over birds with golden plumage, and they fly off with it. From above they speak: "O thou of small sense, we are even those dice." Zhukovsky's Russian version adds a parting line: "farewell, reckless one; a happy journey!" That is how The Fool is born: a man at zero whose own dice wish him a good road. The couple's main task is what two people do when they have nothing.

The tale gives both answers. In the plus, the two walk on "both attired in one cloth": one cloth for two, and that is enough. In the minus, at night Nala decides his wife will be better off without him, cuts their shared cloth in half and leaves. The centre of every such couple is Justice, an atmosphere of scales: fair, equal, each paying their own way. **The most dangerous thing this tail knows how to do is to split everything equally and leave "for the other's good".** Nala decided for both of them and did not ask.

Nala turns into a homely stableman; Damayanti sends messengers out with the question "O beloved gambler, where hast thou gone?" To bring him back she announces a new choice of husband, and her maid reports on the strange stableman: vessels fill with water at his glance, grass bursts into flame in his hand, a withered rose comes back to life. Zhukovsky names the answer outright: "these were the gifts he had received from the gods on his very wedding day, and she… saw with her heart the longed-for Nala where her eyes still saw Vahuka." The last test is a piece of meat cooked by the stableman.

**The dice took the kingdom, the clothes and even his face, but not the wedding gifts.** Waite has a strange thought about Justice, the card at this couple's centre: the law deals with each according to his works, while gifts "we have them or have not". The law of stakes takes whatever has been staked. A gift is never put on the table. This couple's Empress is not a flat or furniture but the ability of the two of them to make life around them alive: to feed, to warm, to bring the withered back. The Tower can take the walls and the familiar image of each other. It does not take the ability to make things grow, and by it the two recognise each other when everything external is already lost.

The night after their meeting, Nala and Damayanti tell each other what each lived through in the forest, and in Zhukovsky "the sad true stories turned into a merry tale". The Fool's task is solved not by a return to the palace but by the forest becoming a shared story.

What helps a couple with this tail: naming the crack aloud while it is small; agreeing in advance on what is never staked; in trouble, not deciding for the other what would be better for them; not splitting everything in half at a moment of fear; looking after the gifts, not just the property; after a hard period, telling each other the story of the "forest".

unit.title: What is never staked

captions.M: To want a living home where everything grows
captions.N: To live through the collapse of what rested on habit
captions.D: To start from zero together, not split in half out of fear

unit.meaning: Your task is to go through loss together: don't decide for each other, don't split everything, guard what you can grow.
